lesson.title: Dividing to Conquer: How Stratified Random Sampling Works
lesson.summary: Stratified random sampling splits a population into homogeneous subgroups called strata and then draws a separate simple random sample from each one, a two step process that can produce more precise estimates than an SRS of the same total size.
lesson.body:
Stratified random sampling begins by dividing the entire population into distinct, non-overlapping subgroups called strata, chosen so that individuals within a given stratum are relatively similar to each other with respect to some characteristic that matters for the study, while individuals in different strata may differ more substantially. Once the strata are defined, the researcher draws a separate simple random sample, an SRS as defined earlier, from within each stratum on its own, and then combines all of those individual stratum samples together into the final overall sample.

A worked example shows the mechanics clearly. Suppose a high school has 900 students total, made up of 300 freshmen, 250 sophomores, 200 juniors, and 150 seniors, and the school wants an overall sample of 90 students to survey about cafeteria food, while making sure every grade level is well represented in proportion to its size. Using proportional stratified sampling, the school takes 10 percent of each grade level as an SRS: an SRS of 30 from the 300 freshmen, since 300 times 0.10 equals 30, an SRS of 25 from the 250 sophomores, an SRS of 20 from the 200 juniors, and an SRS of 15 from the 150 seniors. Adding these together, 30 plus 25 plus 20 plus 15 equals exactly 90, the desired total sample size, and every grade is represented in the same proportion it holds in the full student body.

The reason this can outperform a plain SRS of the same total size, 90 students drawn straight from all 900 without regard to grade, is grounded in how sampling variability works. If opinions about cafeteria food genuinely differ by grade level, perhaps seniors who can leave campus for lunch feel differently than freshmen who cannot, then a plain SRS of 90 students could, purely by bad luck, end up with too few seniors or too many freshmen, skewing the overall result. Stratifying by grade guarantees the right number from each grade every single time, removing that particular source of chance imbalance entirely and typically shrinking the margin of error compared to a plain SRS of equal size, provided the strata truly do differ on the variable being studied.

It is important to see how this design builds directly on the simple random sample rather than replacing it. Inside each stratum, freshmen, sophomores, juniors, and seniors alike, the actual selection of individuals is still carried out using an ordinary SRS, complete with numbered labels and a random number generator exactly as described before. Stratification changes how the population is organized before sampling begins; it does not change the fundamentally random, equal-chance mechanism used to pick individuals once inside a given group.

Stratified sampling also does not have to be proportional the way the cafeteria example was. A researcher can deliberately oversample a small stratum, such as taking a much larger fraction of a rare subgroup than its share of the population would suggest, in order to get enough data to say something precise about that subgroup specifically, and then adjust the combined estimates mathematically to account for the different sampling fractions. Whether proportional or not, the defining feature remains the same: separate, deliberate simple random samples drawn from within meaningfully different subgroups of the population, then combined.
